organism: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA betacoronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China in December 2019. Its surface spike (S) protein binds the human ACE2 receptor to enter cells and is the primary target of vaccine-induced immunity. SARS-CoV-2 evolves continually through antigenic drift, producing a succession of variants (e.g. Alpha, Delta, and the still-circulating and diversifying Omicron lineage) that can partially evade immunity from prior infection or vaccination - the reason vaccine composition is reviewed and updated on a roughly annual cycle, similar to influenza vaccine.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is typically 2-5 days for more recent Omicron-lineage variants (longer, around 4-6 days, for earlier variants). Presentation ranges from asymptomatic infection through mild upper respiratory illness (fever, cough, sore throat, congestion, fatigue, myalgia, headache, and loss of taste/smell, the last more characteristic of earlier variants than current ones) to severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, multiorgan involvement, and death. Risk of severe disease rises sharply with age and is also elevated by obesity, diabetes, chronic cardiopulmonary/renal/liver disease, immunocompromise, and pregnancy. Some people experience persistent or delayed symptoms weeks to months after acute infection (post-COVID conditions/"long COVID"), and children can rarely develop multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C) several weeks after infection.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the primary reservoir, though SARS-CoV-2 also infects and can circulate in some animal species (e.g. deer, mink), raising some concern about spillback and novel-variant emergence outside human surveillance. Transmission is primarily via respiratory droplets and aerosols from close contact, with airborne transmission in poorly ventilated indoor spaces also documented; fomite transmission is possible but considered a minor contributor. Unlike influenza, COVID-19 has not settled into a strictly seasonal pattern in the US, though winter activity has generally been higher; distinct waves have been driven by the emergence of new, more transmissible or immune-evasive variants rather than by season alone. Infectiousness typically begins shortly before symptom onset (or from the time of a positive test in asymptomatic infection) and declines over the following week, though it varies by variant, vaccination status, and immune status.
secularTrendsSummary: The COVID-19 pandemic, declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in January 2020 and a national emergency in the US shortly after, caused the largest US infectious-disease mortality event in over a century - more than 1 million reported US deaths through the acute pandemic period, with case counts and deaths falling substantially after 2022 as population immunity (from vaccination and prior infection) built up and variants shifted toward somewhat lower average severity. The US public health emergency declaration ended in May 2023. COVID-19 has since transitioned toward endemic, wave-like circulation rather than the sharp epidemic peaks of 2020-2022, though it continues to cause substantial seasonal hospitalization and mortality, concentrated in older adults and people with underlying conditions - a burden comparable to or exceeding a typical influenza season in many recent years.
vaccineDescription: Two vaccine platforms are currently licensed in the US: mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech's Comirnaty and Moderna's Spikevax, plus Moderna's newer mNEXSPIKE, which encodes only the spike protein's receptor-binding and N-terminal domains rather than the full protein) and a protein subunit vaccine (Novavax's Nuvaxovid, containing spike protein with a saponin-based adjuvant). All are given intramuscularly. Formulation is updated roughly annually - similar to influenza vaccine - to better match circulating variants; because of this, product availability, exact age indications, and the specific variant targeted all change from season to season, and this chapter's schedule/safety/contraindication summaries describe the general, recurring pattern rather than any single season's specific formulation (see Annual Reformulation).
vaccinationScheduleSummary: As of this chapter's most recent check (see Active Litigation Over COVID-19 Vaccine Policy - verify current status before relying on this), the operative recommendation is: annual vaccination for all adults 18 and older; routine annual vaccination (with additional doses permitted through shared clinical decision-making) for children and adolescents 6 months through 17 years who are moderately or severely immunocompromised; and vaccination via shared clinical decision-making - a discussion between patient/parent and provider weighing individual risk and preference, rather than a blanket recommendation - for other children 6 months through 17 years. Number of doses and intervals for a given season depend on age, product, and prior vaccination history (e.g., an unvaccinated young child may need 2-3 doses of the current season's vaccine rather than 1); a previously vaccinated person generally needs 1 dose of the current formulation, at least 2 months (immunocompromised) to 8 weeks (others) after their most recent dose.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Vaccine effectiveness against symptomatic infection is moderate and wanes over months, particularly as new variants emerge that partially evade immunity from earlier formulations - the same basic dynamic that drives influenza's annual reformulation cycle, though COVID-19 variants have historically evolved and spread faster. Effectiveness against severe disease, hospitalization, and death is substantially higher and more durable than effectiveness against any infection or symptomatic illness. Updated (variant-matched) vaccine doses restore and typically exceed the protection provided by earlier formulations against currently circulating strains. Hybrid immunity (vaccination plus prior infection) generally produces broader and more durable protection than either alone.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) after a previous dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, or to any component, is a contraindication to that same platform; a diagnosed, non-severe allergy (e.g. urticaria confined to the injection site) is a precaution rather than a contraindication. Moderate or severe acute illness is a general precaution. A history of myocarditis or pericarditis not attributed to a prior COVID-19 vaccine dose is not itself a contraindication, but a history of myocarditis/pericarditis following a prior mRNA COVID-19 vaccine dose is a precaution for a subsequent mRNA dose specifically (see Myocarditis and Pericarditis Risk) - the protein-subunit Novavax vaccine is an alternative to consider in that situation, given its different mechanism.
vaccineSafetySummary: Most adverse reactions are the common, self-limited local and systemic reactions typical of injectable vaccines: injection-site pain, fatigue, headache, myalgia, chills, and fever, generally resolving within a few days and somewhat more frequent after an mRNA vaccine than after Novavax. The most clinically significant identified safety signal is myocarditis and pericarditis following mRNA vaccination, occurring most often in adolescent and young adult males, typically within a week after a second dose, usually mild and self-limited with supportive care, and less common after updated/subsequent doses than after the primary series. ACIP has repeatedly reviewed this signal and concluded that the benefits of vaccination continue to outweigh this risk for recommended populations, though patients (especially males 12-39) should be counseled about it. Large-scale postlicensure safety monitoring (VAERS, Vaccine Safety Datalink, and other systems) has not identified other serious safety signals disproportionate to the vaccinated population's size.
vaccineStorageSummary: Storage requirements are product-specific and have been revised repeatedly since initial licensure - current mRNA formulations generally allow standard refrigerator storage (2C to 8C / 36F to 46F) for substantial periods, a significant simplification from the ultra-cold-chain requirements of the original 2020-2021 formulations, though manufacturer-specific details (beyond-use dating after thawing or first puncture, freezer options) still vary by product. Novavax requires refrigerator storage. Always check the current manufacturer package insert and CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit rather than relying on a prior season's requirements.
surveillanceSummary: COVID-19 has been a nationally notifiable condition since April 2020, with both confirmed and probable cases reportable (probable cases only from lower-incidence jurisdictions, per CSTE's 2022 position statement). COVID-19-associated pediatric mortality became a separately nationally notifiable condition in 2026. Diagnosis relies on nucleic acid amplification testing (e.g. RT-PCR) or antigen testing; the specific case definitions and testing recommendations have been revised multiple times since 2020 as the pandemic's phase and testing technology changed. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases and NNDSS for current reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Active Litigation Over COVID-19 Vaccine Policy (Verify Before Relying on This Chapter)
supplementalTopics.summary: COVID-19 vaccine recommendations are, as of this chapter's curation (September 2026), more legally and administratively unsettled than any other chapter in this library. Starting in June 2025, ACIP's membership and processes were restructured under new HHS leadership; a May 2025 HHS announcement (preceding that restructuring) downgraded the pediatric COVID-19 recommendation from universal to shared clinical decision-making for children without qualifying immunocompromise, and further changes followed through late 2025 and into January 2026. On March 16, 2026, a federal judge (Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass., in litigation brought by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical societies) issued a stay blocking the January 2026 schedule overhaul and the ACIP restructuring itself, reverting the immunization schedule toward its earlier state - but the May 2025 COVID-19 shared-clinical-decision-making change was specifically named as remaining in effect despite that stay, which is why VaccinationScheduleSummary above reflects that framework rather than a full universal recommendation. As of September 2026, this litigation remains active and unresolved: the case is paused at the district court pending a First Circuit Court of Appeals ruling on the government's appeal, with oral argument scheduled for October 6, 2026. This means the legal and administrative status of COVID-19 vaccine recommendations could change again on short notice, in either direction, independent of any new clinical evidence. Anyone using this chapter for an actual vaccination decision should check CDC's live COVID-19 vaccine guidance and current litigation status directly rather than trusting this chapter's snapshot - more so than for any other topic in this library.

supplementalTopics.title: Myocarditis and Pericarditis Risk
supplementalTopics.summary: Myocarditis/pericarditis following mRNA COVID-19 vaccination was first identified as a signal in mid-2021, concentrated in males 12-29, most often within a week after the second dose of a primary series, with typical presentation of chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations. Most cases have been mild, resolved with conservative treatment (rest and anti-inflammatory medication), and had a favorable short-term clinical course, though long-term outcome data are still accumulating. Reported rates have been highest after a primary-series second dose in adolescent/young adult males (on the order of several to about 10 cases per 100,000 doses in the highest-risk groups) and substantially lower after booster/updated doses. ACIP has reviewed this signal multiple times (first formally on June 23, 2021) and has consistently concluded that vaccination's benefits - including protection against COVID-19-associated myocarditis, which occurs more frequently and often more severely than vaccine-associated myocarditis - outweigh the risk for its recommended populations, while directing that affected patients be counseled about it.

supplementalTopics.title: Annual Reformulation - A Living Recommendation
supplementalTopics.summary: Like influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine composition is reviewed and reissued roughly annually (generally in the spring/summer for the following fall-winter season) based on circulating and anticipated SARS-CoV-2 variants - the 2024-2025 season targeted the KP.2 lineage, and subsequent seasons have continued to update the target strain as the virus has evolved (e.g. toward JN.1-descendant lineages). Beyond variant matching, product labels, specific age indications, and which manufacturers have an approved or authorized product for a given season have also changed from year to year. Treat the schedule, safety, and contraindication summaries here as describing the general, recurring pattern rather than a fixed formulation, and check CDC's current-season guidance (https://www.cdc.gov/covid/hcp/vaccine-considerations/) for the specifics of any given year - keeping in mind the additional legal uncertainty described in Active Litigation Over COVID-19 Vaccine Policy.

keyPoints: SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in December 2019; the WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in January 2020, and the US ended its own public health emergency declaration in May 2023
COVID-19 caused more than 1 million reported US deaths through the acute pandemic period - the largest US infectious-disease mortality event in over a century
Vaccine composition is reviewed roughly annually to match evolving variants, similar to influenza vaccine, and the specific formulation/product availability changes every season
Vaccine effectiveness against severe disease and death is substantially higher and more durable than effectiveness against infection or mild illness

Myocarditis/pericarditis after mRNA vaccination is a real but rare, mostly mild and self-limited signal, concentrated in young males after a second primary-series dose - ACIP has repeatedly concluded the benefits outweigh this risk for recommended populations

As of September 2026, COVID-19 vaccine policy is under active, unresolved federal litigation (a March 2026 court stay, currently on appeal with an October 6, 2026 hearing) - this chapter's schedule reflects the currently operative guidance, not a settled, permanent recommendation, and should be verified against CDC's live pages before being relied on
COVID-19 has been nationally notifiable since April 2020; COVID-19-associated pediatric mortality became separately nationally notifiable in 2026
